items.title: The Rain Rule
items.question: If it rains, the match is cancelled. It rained this morning. What necessarily follows?
items.correctExplanation: Exactly. This is modus ponens: the rule guarantees cancellation whenever rain happens, and rain happened.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is: the match is off. The conditional 'if rain then cancelled' plus the fact of rain forces the conclusion by modus ponens. Any other option quietly denies a premise.
items.lessonContent:
Modus ponens is the simplest guaranteed-valid argument form: if P then Q; P; therefore Q.
Logicians call it affirming the antecedent — the rule's trigger fires, so the consequence must follow.
Its power is unconditional: once both premises hold, the conclusion cannot fail.
Refund policies, warranties and cancellation rules are all written as conditionals, and applying them is pure modus ponens.
Share this: next time a policy says 'if X then Y' and X happens, ask a friend whether Y is now guaranteed.

items.title: The Alarm Test
items.question: If the alarm works, it beeps when tested. It did not beep when tested. What can you conclude?
choices: The alarm never beeps at all
items.correctExplanation: Correct — modus tollens. A working alarm would have beeped; the silence rules out the working alarm.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is: the alarm is not working. Since a functional alarm must beep on test, the missing beep eliminates that possibility — modus tollens in action. A dead battery is a possible cause, but it is an extra guess the premises never mention.
items.lessonContent:
Modus tollens runs a conditional backwards by negation: if P then Q; not Q; therefore not P.
It is the logical engine of debugging — a missing expected effect eliminates the assumed cause.
Scientists use it constantly: a failed prediction kills the hypothesis that predicted it.
The only trap is confirming that Q truly failed — silence only counts when silence is impossible.
Share this: when something expected doesn't happen, trace which if-then rule just got falsified.

items.title: Wet Ground Logic
items.question: If it rained, the ground is wet. The ground is wet. Is the conclusion 'it rained' logically valid?
choices: Yes — wet ground proves rain fell
Yes — rain is the only source of moisture
No — something else could have wet it
No — the ground must be dry
items.correctAnswer: No — something else could have wet it
items.correctExplanation: Right — this is the fallacy of affirming the consequent. The rule runs from rain to wet, not backwards.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is no: something else could have wet it. A sprinkler, a hose, or a spilled bucket all produce wet ground without rain. Affirming the consequent treats 'if P then Q' as if it were 'if Q then P', which is exactly the trap here.
items.lessonContent:
Affirming the consequent is the classic broken inference: if P then Q; Q; therefore P.
The rule points one way, but the effect usually has many possible makers.
Doctors and detectives live inside this gap daily: a symptom fits a cause without proving it.
The repair is asking what else produces the same effect before committing to one explanation.
Share this: catch one headline today that assumes a single cause and ask aloud what else fits.

items.title: Missed the Train
items.question: If you catch the 8:00 train, you arrive by noon. You missed the 8:00 train. Does it follow that you cannot arrive by noon?
choices: Yes — she cannot arrive by noon
Yes — noon arrival requires that exact train
No — another route could still arrive by noon
items.correctAnswer: No — another route could still arrive by noon
items.correctExplanation: Correct — denying the antecedent. The rule only promises the noon arrival for that train; it says nothing about other ways to arrive.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is no: another route could still arrive by noon. The premise guarantees that the 8:00 train suffices, never that it is necessary — denying the antecedent treats sufficiency as if it were exclusivity.
items.lessonContent:
Denying the antecedent mistakes a sufficient condition for a necessary one: if P then Q; not P; therefore not Q.
The rule never said P was the only route to Q — other doors may stand open.
'Guaranteed by' and 'only achievable through' are different claims entirely.
Schedule logic, guarantees and eligibility rules all run on this distinction.
Share this: reread one guarantee today and ask whether it promises sufficiency or exclusivity.

items.title: The Chain Rule
items.question: Every emerald is harder than every opal. Every opal is harder than every pearl. If E is an emerald and P is a pearl, what follows?
choices: E and P are equally hard
items.correctExplanation: Yes — hardness chains by transitivity: emerald over opal, opal over pearl, so emerald over pearl.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is: E is harder than P. 'Harder than' is transitive — if E outranks the opal and the opal outranks the pearl, E outranks the pearl. Any other ranking reverses or ignores the chain.
items.lessonContent:
Transitivity lets relations chain: if A outranks B and B outranks C, then A outranks C.
Not every relation obeys it — 'beats' in rock-paper-scissors famously loops instead of chaining.
Orderings like taller than, earlier than and heavier than chain safely; preferences and pairwise votes can cycle.
Spotting which relations transfer is a quiet superpower in rankings and comparisons.
Share this: next time you see a ranking, ask whether the relation actually chains or just loops.

items.title: The Shared Label
items.question: All chess players are strategists. All generals are strategists. Does it follow that all chess players are generals?
choices: Yes — both groups use strategy daily
Yes — one strategist group contains the other
No — the middle term is undistributed
No — chess players are not strategists
items.correctAnswer: No — the middle term is undistributed
items.correctExplanation: Correct. Both groups merely sit inside 'strategists' — nothing says they overlap each other.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is no: the middle term is undistributed. Sharing a category with something does not put you inside it — that is the fallacy of the undistributed middle. The premises place chess players and generals inside 'strategists' but never connect the two groups directly.
items.lessonContent:
The undistributed middle is the shared-category trap: all A are C; all B are C; therefore all A are B.
Both groups live inside the same tent, but the tent's floor plan never connects them.
Venn-diagram thinking defuses it instantly — draw the big circle and watch the two groups drift apart inside it.
The same trap powers stereotypes: sharing one label with a group says nothing about overlapping further.
Share this: catch one 'they're all the same' claim today and name the shared tent doing the work.

items.title: Mutual Exclusion
items.question: 'No ghosts are physicists.' Which statement follows with certainty?
items.correctExplanation: Exactly — E-propositions convert cleanly: mutual exclusion runs both directions.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is: no physicists are ghosts. 'No A are B' converts to 'No B are A' because exclusion is symmetric. The other options sneak in existence or overlap that the premise never grants.
items.lessonContent:
'No A are B' converts cleanly to 'No B are A' — exclusion is symmetric, so the flip costs nothing.
Conversion is safe for exclusions and for 'some' statements, the two shapes logic can flip without loss.
Universals of the 'all' type do not convert — flipping those is the illicit move.
Knowing which statements flip is half of traditional syllogistic craft.
Share this: take one 'no X are Y' claim you hear and enjoy that it reverses for free.

items.title: Overlap Proof
items.question: 'Some poets are engineers.' What follows necessarily?
items.correctExplanation: Right — partial overlap is symmetric: the same people counted from either side.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is: some engineers are poets. If at least one person is both, then reading the overlap from the engineering side gives the same result — I-propositions convert. Widening 'some' to 'all' or denying the overlap both overstate the premise.
items.lessonContent:
'Some A are B' converts as well: the overlap is the very same people counted from either side.
This is why partial-overlap statements feel reversible — one direction hands you the other.
The conversion preserves quantity: 'some' never inflates to 'all' or collapses to 'none' by flipping.
Careful reading of surveys and statistics is mostly careful tracking of which direction was claimed.
Share this: find one 'some' claim today and state its converse — notice it costs you nothing.

items.title: The Reverse Trap
items.question: 'All drones are machines.' Which statement is NOT guaranteed by this alone?
choices: Every drone counts as a machine
Drones belong to the machine family
items.correctExplanation: Correct — reversing a universal is illicit. The premise puts drones inside machines, not the other way around.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is: 'all machines are drones' is not guaranteed. 'All A are B' never implies 'All B are A' — that is illicit conversion. The other options merely restate or weaken the original claim, which is always safe.
items.lessonContent:
'All A are B' cannot be flipped: B is usually the larger set, and A merely sits inside it.
Logicians call the flip illicit conversion — swapping subject and predicate of a universal breaks it.
The classic instance: all roses are flowers, yet not all flowers are roses.
Subset-to-superset is a one-way street; remember it and half of category errors vanish.
Share this: catch one category flip in conversation today and gently reverse it back.

items.title: The Age Chain
items.question: All kids are learners. All learners are curious. All curious minds ask questions. If Mia is a kid, what follows?
items.correctExplanation: Yes — the chain links kid to learner to curious to questioner, so membership travels all the way down.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is: Mia asks questions. This is a sorites — three universal links chained together — and each one carries Mia's membership forward. The other options break a link the premises never break.
items.lessonContent:
A sorites chains several universals into one conveyor: A to B to C to D carries membership the whole way.
The name is Greek for heap — the original puzzle asked when grains become a heap.
Each link must be universal; a single 'some' or 'most' anywhere breaks the chain's guarantee.
Long eligibility rules and cascading requirements are sorites in the wild.
Share this: pick one multi-step requirement you know and check whether every link truly says 'all'.

items.title: Two Doors
items.question: Either the butler or the gardener opened the door last night. The gardener was locked outside all evening. Who did it?
items.correctExplanation: Exactly — a disjunctive syllogism. With one option eliminated, the other must hold.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is: the butler opened it. The premise offers exactly two candidates; eliminating the gardener leaves the butler by pure elimination. 'Cannot be determined' ignores that the disjunction named the only possible openers.
items.lessonContent:
A disjunctive syllogism eliminates: either P or Q; not P; therefore Q.
It is the logic of process-of-elimination — the surviving option wins by default, not by direct evidence.
The move only works if the either-or genuinely exhausts the possibilities.
Sherlock Holmes called the exhaustive version his method: remove the impossible and whatever remains must be the truth.
Share this: next time you eliminate options, ask whether the list was ever complete to begin with.

items.title: The Negative Pair
items.question: No cats are dogs. No dogs are felines. Does 'no cats are felines' follow?
choices: Yes — the chain of negatives transfers downward
No — this pattern is structurally invalid
Yes — exclusion spreads to overlapping groups
No — one premise must mention felines twice
items.correctAnswer: No — this pattern is structurally invalid
items.correctExplanation: Correct — two negative premises connect nothing. Cats and felines stay unlinked by these premises.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is no — this pattern is structurally invalid. Two negative premises cannot yield any conclusion about how cats and felines relate; in fact cats are felines, which shows how wrong the chain of negatives is. Classical logicians flagged this as the exclusive-premises rule.
items.lessonContent:
Two negative premises prove nothing about connection — they only state what excludes what.
Classical logicians banned pairs of 'no' statements from yielding any conclusion: the exclusive-premises rule.
The reason is structural: nothing bridges the two terms that need relating.
The cat-and-feline counterexample shows why — nature had already settled what the logic forbids concluding.
Share this: when you meet two 'no' statements in a row, pause before trusting whatever follows.

items.title: Ticket to Enter
items.question: Having a ticket is necessary to board. Riya has a ticket. Can she definitely board?
choices: No — some tickets can be fake at the gate
No — the ticket permits boarding but doesn't guarantee it
items.correctAnswer: No — the ticket permits boarding but doesn't guarantee it
items.correctExplanation: Right — necessary is not sufficient. A ticket removes one barrier; other conditions can still block boarding.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is no: the ticket permits boarding but doesn't guarantee it. 'Necessary' means 'without it, no boarding' — not 'with it, boarding'. Gate closures, lost seats, or a second requirement can all still stop her. Confusing necessary with sufficient is one of the most common reasoning errors.
items.lessonContent:
Necessary means without it, impossible; sufficient means with it, guaranteed.
The two are mirror images, and most real requirements are necessary but not sufficient.
Degrees for jobs, keys for engines and tickets for entry all follow the same asymmetry.
Asking 'is this a must-have or a game-ender?' sorts requirements instantly.
Share this: list one thing you treat as sufficient today and check whether it is merely necessary.

items.title: The Contrapositive
items.question: 'All metals conduct electricity.' Which statement is logically equivalent?
choices: Nothing that fails to conduct electricity is a metal
All conductors of electricity are metals
Some metals do not conduct electricity
items.correctAnswer: Nothing that fails to conduct electricity is a metal
items.correctExplanation: Correct — contraposition. 'All A are B' and 'All non-B are non-A' say the same thing from opposite ends.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is: nothing that fails to conduct electricity is a metal. Flipping and negating both sides preserves the meaning exactly — contraposition. Reversing without negating (option two) is illicit conversion, and option three contradicts the premise outright.
items.lessonContent:
Contraposition is the one transformation that preserves a universal exactly: all A are B equals all non-B are non-A.
It flips and negates both sides — doing only one of those breaks the equivalence.
Contrapositives power indirect proof: to show something belongs, show it cannot belong to the complement.
Insurance clauses and eligibility rules often hide their contrapositive form in plain sight.
Share this: take one 'only members may enter' sign and state its contrapositive aloud.

items.title: Only Members
items.question: Only members can enter the vault. Ravi just entered the vault. What follows?
items.correctExplanation: Exactly — 'only members enter' reverses the direction: entering forces membership.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is: Ravi is a member. 'Only A can B' means 'whoever B's is an A' — so entering the vault certifies Ravi as a member. The 'only' flips the conditional's direction, and missing that flip is the classic trap.
items.lessonContent:
'Only A are B' translates to 'all B are A' — the 'only' reverses the direction of containment.
'Only members may enter' means every enterer is a member; it never means every member enters.
Mistranslating 'only' is among the most common logic slips in exams and contracts alike.
The fix is mechanical: rewrite the sentence as 'all ... are ...' before reasoning about it.
Share this: find one 'only' sentence today and rewrite it the all-way before deciding what it promises.

items.title: The Bell Condition
items.question: You may leave only if the bell rings. The bell did not ring. What follows?
items.correctExplanation: Correct — 'only if' makes the bell a requirement, and a failed requirement blocks the permission.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is: you may not leave. 'Leave only if bell' means leaving requires the bell — with no bell, leaving is off the table. This is modus tollens applied to the 'only if' translation, which many readers misread as 'if bell then may leave'.
items.lessonContent:
'P only if Q' means Q is a requirement for P: without Q, no P.
It translates as 'if P then Q' — pointing forward from the action to its requirement.
Contrast 'if Q then P', which makes the requirement itself sufficient — the exact reversal.
Contracts and permissions are full of only-if clauses doing quiet work.
Share this: find one 'only if' in a rule you follow and translate it the if-then way.

items.title: The Unicorn Count
items.question: 'All dragons are fire-breathers.' Which inference commits the existential fallacy?
choices: Dragons that exist would breathe fire
items.correctExplanation: Right — 'all dragons are X' is vacuously true if no dragons exist, so it cannot promise that any fire-breathing dragon actually exists.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is: 'some fire-breathers are dragons'. A universal claim about dragons says nothing about dragons existing — 'some' assertions demand existence. Assuming existence from a universal is the existential fallacy, the exact gap between traditional and modern logic.
items.lessonContent:
Universals carry no existence promise: 'all dragons breathe fire' is vacuously true if dragons don't exist.
The existential fallacy squeezes a 'some' out of an 'all' — inventing members the premise never delivered.
Modern logic keeps universals existence-free, which is why 'some' claims need their own evidence.
The gap matters in law and data alike: a rule about all cases says nothing about any case existing.
Share this: catch one 'so there must be some' inference today and ask who proved the 'some'.

items.title: Perfect Form, False Fact
items.question: All planets are stars. Mars is a planet. Therefore Mars is a star. How is this argument best described?
choices: Valid and sound — Mars is a star
Valid but unsound — form holds, premise false
Invalid — the conclusion contradicts the premises
items.correctAnswer: Valid but unsound — form holds, premise false
items.correctExplanation: Exactly. Validity is about form; soundness adds true premises. The form is perfect — the astronomy is not.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is: valid but unsound — form holds, premise false. The conclusion follows the premises flawlessly, which makes it valid; but 'all planets are stars' is false, which breaks soundness. Validity and truth are separate judgements — an argument can be impeccably built on rubbish.
items.lessonContent:
Validity is about shape: if the premises were true, the conclusion could not fail.
Soundness stacks truth on top: a sound argument is valid and actually has true premises.
A valid argument can therefore conclude nonsense — built perfectly on a false floor.
The two axes are independent, and judging them separately is the first discipline of logic.
Share this: take one argument you admire and grade it twice — once for form, once for facts.

items.title: The Broken Link
items.question: If A then B. If B then C. If C then D. We know A. An intern claims: 'So D.' Is the intern right?
choices: Yes — each link carries A to D
Yes — but only if D causes A
items.correctAnswer: Yes — each link carries A to D
items.correctExplanation: Correct — hypothetical syllogism. Conditionals chain forward: A reaches B, B reaches C, C reaches D.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is yes: each link carries A to D. Chained conditionals transmit truth forward — that is the hypothetical syllogism, the conditional cousin of the sorites. The intern deserves the credit; the skepticism misreads how forward-chaining works.
items.lessonContent:
Chained conditionals transmit forward: if A then B, if B then C, if C then D lets A reach D.
This is the hypothetical syllogism — the conditional conveyor belt.
The chain is only as strong as its weakest link: one false conditional severs the whole path.
Cascading consequences in code, law and dominoes all follow this exact structure.
Share this: trace one if-then chain in your own plans and find its weakest link.

items.title: The Majority Rule
items.question: Most runners are early risers. Most early risers drink tea. Does it follow that most runners drink tea?
choices: No — the overlaps may barely intersect
items.correctAnswer: No — the overlaps may barely intersect
items.correctExplanation: Right — 'most' does not chain. Two 60% overlaps can share as little as 20% of the group.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is no: the overlaps may barely intersect. Two majorities can cross in a small zone — if 60% of runners rise early and 60% of those risers drink tea, as few as 36% of runners might be tea drinkers. Only universals ('all') chain safely; 'most' leaks.
items.lessonContent:
'All' chains safely; 'most' leaks. Two majorities can cross in a minority of the group.
If most of a club cycles and most of the cyclists also swim, the overlap can still be a small corner of the club.
This quantifier slippage powers many a misleading statistic.
The safe rule: only universals compose; qualified claims need explicit overlap math.
Share this: next time two 'most' claims stack in an argument, do the overlap arithmetic aloud.

items.title: The Border Check
items.question: Every swan in this park is white. A black swan arrives and it is a swan. What must be true?
choices: This swan is white despite appearances
This swan came from somewhere else
items.correctAnswer: This swan came from somewhere else
items.correctExplanation: Correct — the premise scopes whiteness to this park only, so a black swan simply originates beyond it.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is: this swan came from somewhere else. The premise is a scoped universal — 'in this park' — and the black swan's existence contradicts nothing outside that scope. Denying the bird's existence or colour fights the very premise the question grants.
items.lessonContent:
Universals often arrive scoped — 'every X in this park', 'all X before Friday' — and the scope is doing real work.
A scoped rule says nothing about the world outside its fence; exceptions outside survive unharmed.
Black swans famously lived outside Europe's 'all swans are white' scope until Australia was explored.
Reading the fence carefully is most of the game in rules and generalizations.
Share this: find one generalization today and ask where its fence actually ends.

items.title: The Broad Brush
items.question: All dogs are animals. Some animals are wild. Does 'some dogs are wild' follow?
choices: Yes — wildness spreads through all animals
No — no dog has ever gone wild
No — the wild animals need not include dogs
Yes — dogs descend from wolves anyway
items.correctAnswer: No — the wild animals need not include dogs
items.correctExplanation: Correct — the 'some animals' may be entirely non-dogs. The conclusion's subject overreaches its premise.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is no: the wild animals need not include dogs. The premises never say which animals are wild — the wild ones could all be bears. Concluding about dogs from an unspecified 'some animals' is the illicit major fallacy in action.
items.lessonContent:
When a conclusion's subject reaches beyond what its premise ever pinned down, the argument overreaches.
Logicians call the worst case illicit process: a term gets used in the conclusion beyond how the premise used it.
The repair is scope-matching: conclusions may only talk about what premises actually fixed.
Headlines generalize from narrow studies through exactly this gap.
Share this: catch one story that generalizes beyond its study and name what the scope excluded.

items.title: The Step Down
items.question: 'All tasks here are urgent.' Assuming tasks here exist, which weaker claim must also hold?
choices: All urgent things are tasks here
items.correctExplanation: Right — subalternation: a universal about existing things drops down to its 'some' version.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is: some tasks here are urgent. If every task is urgent and at least one task exists, then at least one urgent task exists — the universal implies its particular. The reversal option commits illicit conversion again, and the negative options contradict the premise.
items.lessonContent:
Subalternation is the safe weakening: 'all' implies 'some', provided members actually exist.
'Every card in this deck is red' hands you 'some cards in this deck are red' for free.
It never reverses — 'some' climbs to nothing, and existence is the quiet assumption doing the work.
Downgrade-from-all is always available; upgrade-from-some never is.
Share this: take one 'all' claim you trust and freely weaken it to 'some' — then notice how rarely the reverse is allowed.

items.title: One Truth Only
items.question: Exactly one of the two switches is on. Switch A is off. What do we know?
items.correctExplanation: Exactly — an exclusive disjunction with one side settled forces the other side.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is: switch B is on. 'Exactly one is on' means one and only one; with A off, B must carry the 'on'. Treating the disjunction as inclusive (option three) or as undecided (option four) misreads 'exactly'.
items.lessonContent:
'Either P or Q' comes in two flavours: inclusive (maybe both) and exclusive (exactly one).
The word 'exactly' upgrades to exclusive — and an exclusive pair with one side settled forces the other.
Logic puzzles lean on this constantly: one truth among candidates, eliminate the rest.
Contracts use it too: 'sole discretion', 'one winner' — exclusivity doing logical work.
Share this: find one 'either-or' today and ask whether it secretly allows both.

items.title: The Silent Shipment
items.question: If the shipment made it onto the truck, it left on time. The shipment did not leave on time. What follows?
items.correctExplanation: Correct — modus tollens. No on-time departure means the truck condition never happened.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is: the shipment missed the truck. A loaded truck forces an on-time departure; the departure failed, so by modus tollens the loading never occurred. 'Nothing follows' ignores that conditionals run backwards when negated correctly.
items.lessonContent:
Failed expectations are information: the effect that never arrived falsifies the cause that promised it.
This backwards elimination is how checklists catch silent failures and how tests kill bugs.
One caveat: the conditional must be airtight — other paths to the same effect break the elimination.
Engineering culture is built on cherishing exactly these silent negatives.
Share this: when something quietly fails to appear, write down which promise just got falsified.
